exposure: Complete uterine rupture in the second and third trimester of pregnancy
outcome: Clinical features (e.g., abdominal pain, hemorrhagic shock, prenatal vaginal bleeding)
Management strategies (e.g., surgical repair, blood transfusion, ICU transfer)
Maternal prognosis (e.g., discharge status, resolution of condition)
Infant prognosis (5-minute Apgar score, perinatal mortality)
cohort: The study included 15 patients who experienced complete uterine rupture during their second or third trimester of pregnancy and were admitted to a hospital between January 2012 and December 2020.
finding: The most common clinical features of complete uterine rupture in the second and third trimester included abdominal pain, inability to lie flat, hemorrhagic shock, prenatal vaginal bleeding, and rupture predominantly in the lower uterus and cervix; additionally, patients with scarless uterine rupture showed a remarkably worse maternal-infant prognosis compared to those with scarred uterine rupture.
gest_age: Second and third trimester (at time of rupture)
